title: When Does an In-House Feedback Analytics Model Stop Being Worth Maintaining?
summary: An in-house feedback analytics model stops being worth maintaining when upkeep stops buying insight. Five signals and a seven-question test.
body_markdown:
The build-versus-buy decision gets argued carefully and documented. The keep-versus-retire decision almost never gets scheduled at all. A team builds a text analytics model. It classifies customer feedback well enough. It runs for two or three years, and nobody is ever asked to defend it again. Working and worth it are different tests, and only one of them gets applied.


An in-house feedback analytics model stops being worth maintaining at the point where the effort to keep it current no longer buys new insight. That point usually arrives well before the model stops working, because three clocks run against it from the day it ships. The language in the feedback drifts. The model underneath it gets retired by the provider who made it. The person who holds the system in their head eventually leaves. None of those is a failure of the build. All three are structural.


Below is what that maintenance consists of, five signals you can check this week, and a test you can run this quarter. Thematic's position, set out further down, is that moving off an in-house model doesn't make the upkeep disappear. It makes it somebody else's engineering problem.


## What "worth maintaining" actually means for a feedback model


Worth maintaining is a ratio, not a verdict on quality. It weighs the cost of keeping a model accurate and trusted against the insight it produces that you couldn't get another way.


[Five costs](https://getthematic.com/insights/cost-to-build-an-ai-feedback-analytics-platform) belong on that side:


- **Retraining and relabeling.** Fresh labeled examples from the current period, not just more data.
- **Evaluation.** Defining what good looks like, building evaluation sets, re-running them after every change.
- **Taxonomy governance.** Deciding when a new theme is real, merging duplicates, restating history so trends stay comparable.
- **Dependency tracking.** Watching the retirement schedule of every model and API the system sits on.
- **Documentation and handover.** Keeping the system legible to someone who didn't build it.


Only the first two usually make it into anyone's plan. The ratio tips when all five start consuming the people hired to find insight.


## What keeping an in-house feedback model running actually requires


**The debt is structural, not a sign of sloppy work.**[Google's 2015 paper](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2015/file/86df7dcfd896fcaf2674f757a2463eba-Paper.pdf) on machine learning (ML) systems remains the foundational treatment: "developing and deploying ML systems is relatively fast and cheap, but maintaining them over time is difficult and expensive." The same paper names the CACE principle, Changing Anything Changes Everything, which is why improving one signal can quietly degrade three others. A decade on, the finding holds. A[2025 study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.12019) in ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology compared 318 ML projects against 318 non-ML projects and found the ML projects carried twice the median percentage of self-admitted technical debt.


**The model decays whether or not anyone touches it.** A 2022 study in[Scientific Reports](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-022-15245-z) aged 128 model and dataset combinations across four industries and observed temporal degradation in 91% of cases. For feedback text the mechanism is plain: customers describe new products with new words.[Google Research](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.06297) measured the natural-word vocabulary of user-generated text shifting by more than a third over six years, and found models pre-trained on the earlier text deteriorated heavily on later years.


**The ground moves on someone else's schedule.** Every major model provider now publishes a retirement policy, and the guaranteed notice is shorter than most roadmaps.


**Provider** **Published commitment**


[Microsoft Foundry / Azure OpenAI](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/concepts/model-retirements) Retirement date set 18 months out at launch, deprecated at 12 months, no extensions granted


[OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/deprecations) At least 6 months for generally available models, 3 months for specialized variants, as little as 2 weeks for preview models


[AWS Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-lifecycle.html) 6-month legacy period on most models, 45 days on some. New fine-tuning jobs stop when the base model goes legacy


[Google Vertex AI](https://docs.cloud.google.com/vertex-ai/generative-ai/docs/learn/model-versions) At least 45 days to migrate


[Anthropic](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations) At least 60 days before retirement


A model you built on inherits a[re-validation project](https://getthematic.com/insights/llm-upgrade-trap) roughly every 12 to 18 months, on a calendar you don't control and can't defer.


**The system has an expiry date attached to a person.** Research on[1,932 open source projects](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1906.08058) found that when all key developers departed, only 41% of those projects continued development at all. A survey of 269 IT professionals put the median halving time for knowledge about a particular file at four months. In one study, a participant described parts of a production pipeline nobody would touch, because the principal developer who understood it had left.


## Five signals the model has stopped earning its keep


You can check all five without building a business case.


1. **The[catch-all bucket](https://getthematic.com/insights/keep-ai-themes-accurate-language-changes) is growing.** New feedback stops matching existing categories cleanly, and the unclassified pile grows month over month.
2. **The categories no longer match the language.** Two issues customers now describe differently keep landing in the same theme, and stakeholders start discounting the numbers.
3. **Nobody will approve a change.** One adjustment means holding too much context at once, so the system gets worked around instead of modified.
4. **Your data scientists are curating themes.** People hired to model are spending their weeks on taxonomy upkeep and data wrangling.
5. **One person is quietly carrying it.** Ask who could re-baseline the model next quarter if that person resigned tomorrow. If the answer is nobody, the expiry date is already set.


Four of those describe the maintenance load, not the accuracy. That's the point. Accuracy is usually the last thing to go.


## Why teams keep maintaining a model they should retire


The reluctance is rarely about the model's value. It's about not wanting the original investment to look wasted.[Arkes and Blumer](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jobhdp/v35y1985i1p124-140.html) showed this experimentally in 1985: people continue an endeavor in proportion to what they've already sunk into it, driven by the desire not to appear wasteful. The spend is gone either way. The only live question is what the next year of maintenance buys.


Retirement is also a named control rather than an admission. The[NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) asks organizations to hold mechanisms to "supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems that demonstrate performance or outcomes inconsistent with intended use." The same framework notes that AI systems "may require more frequent maintenance and triggers for conducting corrective maintenance due to data, model, or concept drift." Planning to decommission is governance hygiene, not defeat.


Gartner's TIME model (Tolerate, Invest, Migrate, Eliminate) scores applications on business value against technical fit, and puts maintainability and skills availability among the technical-fit criteria. A feedback model can deliver real value and still be held by one person, running on a model with a published retirement date. That isn't an Eliminate. It's a Migrate. The distinction tells a team who built something useful that they were[right to build it](https://getthematic.com/insights/ai-feedback-analytics-build-buy-matrix) and are now right to move it.


## What changes when you hand the maintenance to a platform


Moving to Thematic doesn't make the upkeep disappear. It stops being yours. Thematic discovers themes from the feedback itself instead of asking you to maintain a predefined taxonomy, so there are no rules or keyword lists to write. Its[Theming Agent](https://getthematic.com/insights/does-thematic-require-manual-theme-tuning) adapts to what customers are currently saying without quarterly rebuilds or analyst intervention, and a dedicated specialist monitors theme quality.


Thematic also fixes what breaks most in-house trend reporting. Merge, rename, or restructure a theme and Thematic re-analyzes all existing feedback against the new structure, so history is[restated under current definitions](https://getthematic.com/insights/keep-feedback-trend-lines-comparable) rather than spliced onto them. Edits save to a draft and only reach the data when someone applies them, with rollback across the last three applied versions. Thematic's own research puts theme discovery at 80% to 90% accuracy before any human refinement.


One limit worth stating plainly: the governance around the taxonomy is still yours to run. That means the owner, the change note, and the stakeholder notice. What moves is the engineering.


## Two teams that reached the threshold


Atlassian's prior approach was a hand-maintained coding frame rather than a model, but the economics are the same. Its research team spent six weeks per cycle bucketing and categorizing feedback in a Miro whiteboard. Those six weeks covered pulse survey data alone, which Atlassian describes as less than 20% of the qualitative data it receives. The full stream runs to roughly 60,000 pieces a month across surveys, community forums, support channels, and in-product responses. Atlassian evaluated 36 vendors before selecting Thematic, and reduced analysis time from weeks to hours. The upkeep had been scaling while the coverage hadn't.


A[large financial services provider](https://getthematic.com/case-studies/financial-services) ran the test the other way around. An analyst built a net promoter score (NPS) agent on an off-the-shelf enterprise large language model in about an hour, from the same survey export. It produced plausible top-level themes. It couldn't give the same answer twice, build a score-change waterfall, or maintain the taxonomy that made month-to-month tracking meaningful. The team concluded that consistency, not summarization, was what they needed. Their technology leadership applied a rule worth borrowing: buy externally for a standalone function, build internally only where the capability is hard to separate from core systems.


## A test you can run this quarter


Answer these about the system you already own. Four come from the Google paper above.


1. How easily could an entirely new approach be tested at full scale?
2. How precisely can you measure the impact of a change?
3. Does improving one theme or signal degrade others?
4. How quickly could a new team member be brought up to speed?
5. When does the model or API you depend on reach its published retirement date?
6. What share of your insight team's time went to upkeep last quarter rather than analysis?
7. If the person who maintains it resigned tomorrow, what happens in the next 90 days?


## The short answer


An in-house feedback analytics model stops being worth maintaining when the effort to keep it current no longer buys insight you couldn't get another way, and that point typically arrives before accuracy visibly fails. The reliable tells are a growing catch-all bucket, data scientists curating themes instead of modeling, and a single person holding the system. Run the seven questions above. If more than two land badly, the decision is Migrate rather than Eliminate, and the sunk cost isn't an argument.
